heading: Harmfulness judgments can be encoded separately from refusal decisions
definition: the model's harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from the refusal decision.
summary: Several independent groups report separable harmfulness and refusal representations, including through causal interventions. Most evidence is correlational and unreviewed, and separation depends on model family and token position.

suggested_status.by_scale: toy: none. <1B: R2, correlational only (decodability after abliteration and geometry: arXiv:2604.18901, arXiv:2603.27412, cDi2IoUNF2). 1-10B: R2, with causal steering, ablation and head zeroing by several groups on Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Mistral (arXiv:2507.11878, arXiv:2603.05773, arXiv:2609.19366, arXiv:2606.16349, 2eoMtzq03h), limited by model family. 10-100B: R2 for separate-position geometry and decodability (arXiv:2608.08032 Sarvam-30B; gh:drewstone Qwen3.5-27B), plus weight-level pruning at 14B (arXiv:2604.09544); contested by same-token collinearity (arXiv:2610.28982, arXiv:2609.35117); no direction-level causal test. >100B: R0 (one GPT-OSS-120B case study, qSmUharVw6: harmful-refusal cosine 0.54 at layer 20; its V5 rows are probing and geometry only).
suggested_status.reason:
The config names no original for V5 (counts: V5.original_sources_linked is empty), and no tested study shares an author with arXiv:2406.11717 (counts: V5.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 0). The study file's V5 source is Zhao et al., arXiv:2507.11878. Per the checker, its Qwen2 reply-inversion steering held with two more templates (Figure 11) and on Llama3 (Figure 12). Its limits_scope verdict on those design choices should therefore be none. Groups other than Zhao's report the separation with causal interventions on 4-9B Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Mistral models. arXiv:2603.05773: vH steering raises Llama MIR from 4.0% to 42.0%, with 9.5% refusals. arXiv:2609.19366: on Qwen, 60.6 pp harm with 1.0% refusal. arXiv:2606.16349: H-only ablation gives HarmBench ASR 0.1675 -> 0.1400 in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct it rises slightly, 0.2625 -> 0.2925, which the authors call less clean. 2eoMtzq03h: zeroing the 'both' detection-head sets changes judged compliance by 0.0 pp [-5.2, +5.2] in Qwen3-8B, -0.3 pp in Gemma-3-4B and 0.0 pp in Gemma-4-E4B. 2eoMtzq03h's record gives tranche T5. The checker places it in T2: its own results mostly support V5, and its critique of the single-direction account is framing. arXiv:2610.30727 reports the separation correlationally across 15 models. Counts: V5.studies_tested = 43; V5.verdicts.supports.studies = 40; V5.verdicts.challenges.studies = 0; V5.verdicts.limits_scope.studies = 17. That last count includes arXiv:2507.11878's reply-inversion verdict, which the checker says should be none. The evidence is mostly correlational: V5.main_rows_by_operation has measurement 219 and probing 35, against addition 50 and removal 29. It is mostly unreviewed: V5.tested_by_review_class has preprint 27 and reviewed 4. The limits are substantial:
- Harm-refusal alignment is high when both are read at one token (arXiv:2610.28982: 0.69-0.86; arXiv:2609.35117: 0.90-0.97 of ceiling in six models).
- Harm-axis injection triggers refusal in Mistral and Qwen (arXiv:2603.05773: 93.2% and 93.8%).
- Zeroing Gemma-3-4B's 23 retained detection heads raises compliance by +5.6 pp [+2.3, +8.9] (2eoMtzq03h).
- Across harm categories, harm attribution and induced refusal are rank-correlated within each model (arXiv:2609.19366, rho 0.81-0.94).
suggested_status.open_questions:
What would change the level:
- A direction-level causal test above 10B that steers the harm and refusal directions separately and measures the model's own judgment.
- A test of whether same-token collinearity (arXiv:2610.28982, arXiv:2609.35117) vs separate-position orthogonality (arXiv:2507.11878, arXiv:2608.08032) comes down to how the refusal direction is defined.
- Evidence on whether the instruction-token harm signal is the model's judgment or a wording feature (arXiv:2610.30727 finds it below TF-IDF). If it is a wording feature, the probe-based support weakens.
- A failed replication of arXiv:2507.11878's reply-inversion steering, or confirmation of arXiv:2610.30727's template-removal finding, would move toward C.
- An explanation of why Qwen2.5-7B harm-direction steering triggers refusal in arXiv:2603.05773 but not in arXiv:2609.19366.
- Verified refusal removal before probing harm in abliterated checkpoints (arXiv:2604.18901, arXiv:2603.27412).

source.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
source.authors: Andy Arditi; Oscar Obeso; Aaquib Syed; Daniel Paleka; Nina Panickssery; Wes Gurnee; Neel Nanda

original_result.result: The original paper did not separate harmfulness from refusal; this version comes from later work.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: GPT-OSS-20B encoded harmfulness nearly orthogonally to its downstream refusal readout.
Llama and Gemma complied with prompts whose representations occupied wholly harmful regions.
Internal harmfulness signals persisted after ablation induced compliance.
Reasoning models recognized harm while complying, and harm steering differed from compliance steering.
Qwen and Llama often recognized low-resource harmful prompts without refusing them.
Harmfulness remained decodable as refusal declined in Tier-3 languages.
Sarvam-30B showed near-orthogonal harm and refusal axes, although harm separation was weak.
Ouro retained readable harmfulness after one-loop execution largely eliminated refusal.
Narrative wrapping reduced Qwen3-1.7B refusal projections while preserving harmfulness separation.
Roleplay jailbreaks preserved request-side harm signals while reversing refusal.
Tool channels raised refusal thresholds despite comparable harmfulness readouts across eight models.
Safety prompts shifted refusal representations without improving harmfulness separation.
Harm and refusal features responded differently to interventions, especially in Llama.
LLaMA and Gemma retained harmfulness signals on jailbreak inputs they complied with.
Abliterated Qwen checkpoints retained harmfulness discrimination, although refusal removal remained unverified.
Selected models and layers separated harm from refusal, including during DAN and PAIR attacks.
Syntax changes increased jailbreak success while harmfulness probe accuracy remained stable.
Multi-turn attacks showed weak alignment between harmfulness and attack-outcome directions.
Benign reasoning training preserved Qwen harmfulness decoding while degrading refusal decoding.
Instruction-token harm readings tracked refusal weakly, while template-token readings tracked it more strongly.
Harmfulness and refusal separated across token positions and steering interventions.
Harmfulness and refusal directions were nearly orthogonal across twelve instruction-tuned models.
Harm and refusal axes separated geometrically and produced different effects under steering.
Harm and refusal representations had low overlap and different ablation effects in aligned models.
Prefill attacks suppressed refusal while preserving high harmfulness scores.
Compliance fine-tuning removed Qwen3.5-27B refusal while preserving harmfulness probe performance.
Category-specific interventions changed harm judgments and refusal by different amounts in Qwen2.5-7B.
Gemma retained separate harmful and harmless clusters during a successful jailbreak.
Refusal and harm detection used largely distinct weights and responded differently to pruning.
Harm detection persisted after refusal-direction orthogonalisation, although refusal removal was unverified.
GPT-OSS-120B represented harmfulness earlier than refusal, with distinct but related directions.
Small Qwen models complied with harmful jailbreaks despite largely separate harm and refusal directions.
Llama detected harmfulness in both accepted and refused prompts, but refusal activation differed.
Detection-head ablation barely changed compliance, and Qwen retained harm detection after abliteration.
Contextual-risk and refusal directions were weakly aligned, although topic confounding complicated interpretation.
Prefill attacks weakened refusal signals while harmfulness remained detectable.
Accepted harmful prompts changed clusters between instruction and post-instruction tokens.
Shuffling reduced GPT-4o-mini refusal more than it changed harm judgments.
Benign fine-tuning increased compliance while preserving harmfulness separation in Llama3-8B-Instruct.
Adaptive Llama retained readable harmfulness when layer interventions reversed refusal.
GPT-OSS-20B harm–refusal separation depended on which refusal readout was measured.
Harm and refusal directions substantially overlapped at decision tokens across five models.
The refusal-driving component tracked harmfulness, while narration formed the separate component.
Harm-projection signs depended on whether directions came from response or prompt tokens.
Gemma-2-9B failures mostly reflected harm-readout errors, with little recognized-but-unrefused harm.
Harm and refusal axes nearly coincided in most models under tool mediation.
Gemma harm features weakened during jailbreaks and could directly influence refusal.
Qwen2.5-7B did not clearly separate jailbreak harmfulness from benign inputs.
Harm–refusal separation varied with model, layer, token position, and attack.
Harm–refusal separation varied by layer, and the separated harm signal was sensitive to wording.
Reply-inversion tests required model-specific templates and different steering spans.
Harmfulness steering strongly triggered refusal in Mistral and Qwen.
Mistral showed weak causal separation, with refusal interventions often producing unusable outputs.
Harm attribution and refusal remained strongly correlated across categories within each model.
Refusal pruning degraded harm judgments and explanations, while Llama detection pruning damaged core ability.
Gemma-3-4B showed partial coupling between harm detection and refusal execution.
Harm recognition disappeared under PAIR despite different refusal outcomes.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: A direction-level causal dissociation (steering or ablating harm and refusal directions separately) at 10-100B. The causal tests with V5 rows are on 2-9B models; arXiv:2505.23556's feature clamping, for example, is on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.1-8B. At 10-100B the only causal test is weight pruning in Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (arXiv:2604.09544), reported from the text without rows. Above 100B there is one steering case study (next item).
untested.basis: counts: V5.coverage_by_operation.addition.by_size has only 1-10B and not stated; V5.coverage_by_operation.removal.by_size has 1-10B 5 and 10-100B 1. The 10-100B entry appears to come from arXiv:2505.23556's rows labelled 'GEMMA-22B [22B]'; the checks confirm the model is Gemma-2-2B (2B), so the entry belongs in 1-10B. arXiv:2604.09544 has V5 verdicts but no rows.

untested.what: Directional ablation of either direction, and any second study, above 100B. The only >100B study is a GPT-OSS-120B case study: harmful-direction d=2.81 (best layers 10 and 9) and cosine 0.54 with refusal at layer 20. It also steers the harmful vector (Appendix A.2, from the text, not V5 rows): compliance on manipulable harmful prompts without prefill rises from 0% at alpha=0 to 69% (24 of 35 prompts) at alpha=-3, monotonically, unlike the refusal vector; the harmful vector produced no AgentHarm tool calls at any alpha. The study uses activation steering only (top-1 or top-3 layers), with no ablation or weight edit.
untested.basis: counts: V5.studies_by_size.>100B = 1; V5.coverage_by_operation.probing.by_size.>100B = 1 and V5.coverage_by_operation.measurement.by_size.>100B = 1; addition, removal and weight_edit have no >100B (the A.2 steering is reported from the text, not in V5 rows). GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5 (arXiv:2511.08367) have size 'not stated' and are tested behaviourally only.

untested.what: Whether the harm/refusal separation exists before safety training. No study measures the separation in a model before safety training or compares base and instruct models on it. The two studies tagged 'base' are not such tests: arXiv:2610.11005's 'base' Qwen3-1.7B is the released safety-aligned model before the authors' AXIS training (bare attack success 16.2-20.4%), and arXiv:2610.15218's Ouro-1.4B is 'base' only as opposed to its Thinking variant; the text does not describe its safety training, and it refuses at full depth (harmful refusal 0.887, gap +0.737). arXiv:2603.27412 reports its harm read (harmful-vs-benign-aggressive AUROC 1.000) in every variant including Base, but measures no refusal.
untested.basis: counts: V5.studies_by_stage.base = 2, from arXiv:2610.11005 R26 and arXiv:2610.15218 R12/R13; the checks find R26's 'base' tag wrong, so this count is one too high. V5.coverage_by_operation.addition.by_stage and removal.by_stage have no base; probing.by_stage.base = 1 and measurement.by_stage.base = 1.

untested.what: The model's own verbal harm judgment after the V1 direction is ablated or abliterated. Studies of abliterated checkpoints measure decodability only: linear harm directions in arXiv:2604.18901, an unsupervised angular anomaly score in arXiv:2603.27412, and a detection-head probe in 2eoMtzq03h. None of the three measures refusal in its abliterated checkpoints, which are mostly community releases. arXiv:2604.18901's abliterated checkpoints are 0.5B-1.3B in its main set, plus Qwen3.5 2B, 4B and 9B (Table 15, Appendix L).
untested.basis: Untested-parts lines of arXiv:2604.18901 (no behavioural refusal or harm-judgment outputs; removal assumed), arXiv:2603.27412 (model's own judgment untested) and gh:drewstone/safety-is-a-policy (harm encoding after direction ablation untested; its probes follow a QLoRA fine-tune only). counts: V5.coverage_by_operation.weight_edit.studies = 1, by_size <1B = 1. Per the checks this understates coverage: arXiv:2604.18901 also has abliterated 2B, 4B and 9B models, and the checker notes arXiv:2603.27412's R1-R4 also look like weight-edit rows (not confirmable from its text).

untested.what: Families other than Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Mistral, GPT-OSS, Phi and Command/Aya: no OLMo, Yi, GLM, DeepSeek, Falcon or non-transformer models (RWKV, Mamba). Recurrent-depth Ouro is the only non-standard architecture.
untested.basis: counts: V5.studies_by_family lists Qwen, Llama, Gemma, other or not stated, Mistral, GPT-OSS, Command/Aya, Phi and GPT (OpenAI API) only.

untested.what: Harm and refusal directions in vision-language models. The only multimodal study extracts no harm or refusal direction. On the open Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (100 refused MM-SafetyBench inputs under SI-attack) it reports internal proxies instead: a layer-averaged intent score (cosine of clean vs shuffled final-token states) and a refusal score (logit-lens cosine to a 50-token refusal vocabulary). Intent stays comparatively stable at mild shuffling while the refusal score drops in middle-to-late layers. GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5 are tested behaviourally, and LLaVA-v1.5 variants get judge-derived scores only.
untested.basis: Untested-parts line of arXiv:2511.08367 (no internal directions). counts: V5.studies_by_family has no LLaVA, so the study's LLaVA-v1.5 results are not in V5 rows.

untested.what: Positions between the instruction and template tokens, and pooled, attention-based or multi-position probes, for the harm-vs-refusal read.

wording_issues.issue: The separation is graded, not binary. Reported cosines run from about 0 to high alignment: Llama-3.1-8B L27 prompt-side +0.00 (arXiv:2607.00572); contextual-risk vs refusal about 0.33 (Llama3.1 8B) and 0.35 (Qwen3 4B) (wwUAUputSg); harmful vs refusal 0.54 in GPT-OSS-120B, described as distinct but related (qSmUharVw6); 0.69-0.86 at the decision token (arXiv:2610.28982). Within each model, harm attribution and induced refusal are rank-correlated (rho 0.81-0.94, arXiv:2609.19366).

Most V5 evidence is linear decodability of harmful vs harmless prompts, not the model's judgment (counts: V5.main_rows_by_operation measurement 219, probing 35, against addition 50 and removal 29). arXiv:2610.30727 (from the text, not rows): Latent Guard's instruction-token read as published ranks harm below TF-IDF on the rewording set Drew (pooled AUROC median 0.62 vs 0.75 for TF-IDF trained on S2000, below it in every model) and has a framing drop of 0.10-0.37 in all 15 models. The study's other instruction-token readers differ: the linear probe beats TF-IDF by +0.060 AUROC (0.809 at S2000), ties the sentence-embedding classifiers, and at S2000 removes the framing drop. The authors read the instruction-token read as a wording-level judgment that embedding classifiers match. arXiv:2603.27412's harmful-vs-benign-aggressive AUROC is 1.000 in every variant including base models. The studies that measure the model's own judgment are arXiv:2507.11878 (reply inversion), arXiv:2603.05773 (Malicious Interpretation Rate), arXiv:2511.08367 and arXiv:2510.20956 (stated classification).

The refusal side is defined in different ways, and the result depends on it. Definitions include a refused-vs-complied outcome direction (arXiv:2610.28982), a harmful-minus-harmless direction at post-instruction tokens, a success/failure label at end of turn (arXiv:2609.38389), and a compliance direction from teacher-forced canned responses (arXiv:2606.00160). In GPT-OSS-20B the V1-style refusal direction is itself harm-loaded (cosine 0.977 at the instruction token; arXiv:2609.14759). In Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ablating the harmful-minus-benign H carrier (layer 31) did not reopen HarmBench ASR (0.1675 -> 0.1400; arXiv:2606.16349). In Qwen3.5-4B the component that drives refusal reads as harm perception (gh:sekinal/jspace-refusal).

The statement does not say at what level the separation holds, and the answer differs by level. The evidence covers token position (arXiv:2507.11878, arXiv:2610.30727), directions at the same position (arXiv:2610.28982 reads them as largely shared), attention heads (2eoMtzq03h), weights (Jaccard <0.033, arXiv:2604.09544) and SAE features (harm features drive refusal features, arXiv:2505.23556). At the head level, 2eoMtzq03h's results depend on which heads are zeroed. Zeroing the 'both' detection-head sets (recruited and erased by abliteration) moves judged compliance by 0.0 pp (Qwen3-8B), -0.3 pp (Gemma-3-4B) and 0.0 pp (Gemma-4-E4B), which is equivalent within +/-5 pp. Other detection-selected sets on Gemma-3-4B move it more: +5.6 pp [+2.3, +8.9] for its 23 retained heads, and +10.1 pp (Holm p = 4e-6) at the k=59 dose rung. The authors say zeroing moves compliance by at most ten points.

The statement reads as true of models in general, but some families or models are coupled or lose the harm read. arXiv:2603.05773 (AmbiguityBench, N=100): vH injection raises the Malicious Interpretation Rate (MIR) from 27.0% to 74.0% in Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and from 8.0% to 96.0% in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The refusal share of MIR responses goes from 0.0% unsteered to 93.2% (Mistral) and 93.8% (Qwen). The text does not say how MIR responses are classed as refusals. In Gemma-3-4B, zeroing the 23 retained detection heads raises judged compliance by +5.6 pp (2eoMtzq03h). arXiv:2606.01196 (Gemma-2-9B, low-resource-language PolyRefuse harmful test prompts, HRL + 32 LRL gated steering): 0.6% of all harmful prompts were classified harmful and still unrefused after direction addition, against a base Gemma LRL harmful refusal of 70.3%. Of the remaining harmful non-refusals, 93.7% were classified harmless, so the gate ablated the direction from them. The authors say threshold calibration would address most Gemma failures. The Qwen2.5-7B harm direction does not separate complied jailbreaks from benign inputs (arXiv:2504.09466).

method_sensitivity.factor: Token position of the read, and the reader used
method_sensitivity.what: In arXiv:2610.30727 (Dbeh, Latent Guard original recipe), the instruction-token read is mostly decoupled from the model's own refusal (Pi +0.04; beta_s 0.14 with consensus held fixed), while the template-token read is coupled (Pi +0.23, beta_s 1.59). Pi is the median over 78 pairs among 13 of the 15 models (OLMoE-1B-7B and Qwen2.5-3B excluded). The reader matters at the instruction token: under consensus control on Dbeh, LG-z and linear-probe beta_s are 0.36 and 0.43. On Drew, all 19 instruction-token readers have Pi 0.05-0.15. In GPT-OSS-20B the refusal direction's standardized cosine to harm is 0.977 at the instruction token vs 0.49 in-trace. The authors attribute the 0.977 partly to overlapping contrasts ('close to tautological'), and their harm read has cosine 0.16 to the downstream refusal read (arXiv:2609.14759). Reading both directions at a single decision token gives cosines of 0.69-0.86 (arXiv:2610.28982).

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct prompt-side harm-refusal cosine is +0.21 at L12 and +0.00 at L27. The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct response side is +0.42 at L12 and +0.69 at L27 (arXiv:2607.00572). Read one layer at a time at the template token, coupling to refusal rises from 40-50% depth on the rewording set Drew (Figure 3). On Dbeh, Pi is <= 0.01 below 30% depth and 0.23-0.26 above 70% (arXiv:2610.30727). In Sarvam-30B, harm-axis separation of refused vs complied generations peaks at d 0.95 (L9), and the cosines are reported at L11 (arXiv:2608.08032).

Different definitions of the refusal side come with different alignment to harm. A refused-vs-complied direction read at the decision token gives cosines of 0.69-0.86 with the harm-contrast direction (arXiv:2610.28982). A channel-neutral refusal axis gives 0.76-0.97 of ceiling (arXiv:2609.35117). A success/failure direction has a cosine with harmfulness that the authors call 'relatively weak', with no number given (Fig. 7 only; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it; arXiv:2609.38389). On one model: Llama-3.1-8B is near-orthogonal by principal angles between the harm and refusal carriers (86.1-89.4 degrees, arXiv:2606.16349) but reaches 0.78 of ceiling in arXiv:2609.35117, where it is one of the two least collinear models.

arXiv:2510.20956 (Appendix J, from the text): for StrongREJECT prompts, perceived-harmfulness directions extracted from response tokens give negative projections (read as safe), while directions from prompt tokens give highly positive ones. This holds in both s1.1-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Sentence-level drops in one CoT (S6, S22) appear under both choices. Cosine and steering were not rerun with prompt-token directions. arXiv:2604.18901 (from the text, no rows): pooling changes both the direction and the projection-out result. On chat-templated input, max-pool (mp) and last-token (lt) directions are 72.6±6.7 and 74.9±9.3 degrees apart. Projecting out the lt/chat wLDA direction and refitting changes AUROC by -0.186 to -0.398 under lt/chat, +0.001 to +0.020 under mp/chat and -0.010 to +0.001 under mp/raw (Table 12). Raw vs chat input does not change the projection-out result, and no raw-vs-chat direction angle is reported. Under lt pooling, raw->chat raises mean AUROC from 0.972 to 0.993 (Table 4).

arXiv:2610.30727 (Appendix A, not in rows) repeats Zhao et al.'s labelling run on 18 models. That run removes the post-instruction template, not the whole chat template. The removal mostly removes the assistant turn rather than eliciting compliance (coherence fit R² 0.88), so the study labels with the full template. In arXiv:2507.11878, reply-inversion templates were adapted per model because some models sometimes answered the instruction instead of the inversion question. Results were consistent across three Qwen2 templates and on Llama3 (Appendix E.2, Figures 11-12), so the template is not shown to change the outcome. The intervention span does matter there. The refusal direction was applied to all tokens and the harm direction to tokens before the inversion question. Applied to instruction tokens only, the refusal direction had minimal effect (Appendix E.1, Figure 10, Qwen2).

method_sensitivity.factor: Attack type, language and prompt set
method_sensitivity.what: Under ArtPrompt the harm read at xinst survives while refusal is lost. Under PAIR the harm read often fails to identify harmful inputs (arXiv:2511.14423, Sec. 5.1). DAN and PAIR continuations keep harm recognition, while CodeAttack shows only moderate recognition (arXiv:2607.00572). On low-resource-language prompts under HRL + 32 LRL gated steering, the recognised-but-unrefused share of the remaining failures is Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 67.8%, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 50.3% and Gemma-2-9B-it 6.3% (arXiv:2606.01196, Table 3; by language in Table 11). Tier-3 refuse rates are Llama3.1-8B 31%, Qwen2.5-7B 50% and AyaExpanse-8B 31%. Tier 1/Tier 2 rates are 80/75% (Llama), 80/88% (Qwen) and 75/75% (Aya) (arXiv:2607.10112). These rates pool all four perturbation types, so they show sensitivity to language tier, not to attack type. The text does not define the 'refuse' figure.

Injecting the execution axis vR raises the keyword-scored refusal rate on benign prompts from a baseline of 0% to: 96% (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Alpaca), 42% (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, Alpaca), 18% (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Alpaca), 64% (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Guanaco), 6% (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, Guanaco) and 28% (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Guanaco) (arXiv:2603.05773, Table 3). Category-residual steering in arXiv:2609.19366 uses alpha 0.25 for Gemma-2-9B-IT and Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct gets alpha 0.6 because 0.25 produced little change there.

In Gemma-3-4B, zeroing the 'both' head set gives -0.3 pp compliance while zeroing the 'retained' set gives +5.6 pp. Its detection AUROC after abliteration ranges 0.81-0.91 across six recipes (2eoMtzq03h, from the verdict). Specific SAE-feature clamping is largely ineffective for Llama, while common refusal features jailbreak (arXiv:2505.23556). Effects of refusal pruning differ between the refusal v2 and Wei et al. strategies (arXiv:2604.09544).
